 The Most Expensive Mistake I See Buyers Make (And How to Avoid It)
Hi Sara,
Guys, please stop handing out your equity ownership like it’s candy. 
I spend a good chunk of my workweek trying to un-mess partnership disasters. 
So here’s the one thing I wish every business owner, buyer, and entrepreneur would stop doing this year:
👉 Bringing on a “partner” too early or too thoughtlessly.
Sounds harmless, right? You find someone smart, they’re excited, you click. Why not share the load? You split the risk, you gain a sounding board, you finally stop annoying your spouse with endless business talk. What could go wrong?
Well…everything.
The Problem with Equity Promises
Most people give away ownership based on potential: “If we build this together, we’ll win together.” But what actually happens is this: one person ends up doing the heavy lifting while the other disappears to become a rock-climbing, kombucha-making, off-the-grid nomad who still collects 50% of the profits forever.
It’s not just frustrating—it’s legally sticky. You can’t just “unpartner” someone because they stopped showing up. You’ll need a court order or a written agreement (that they’re willing to sign), and those aren’t easy to get. It’s often referred to as a business divorce—and not just for the emotional mess it leaves behind.
What Disgruntled Founders Try Instead:

Spin up a competing business and channel all your energy there (not without risk).

Crank up your salary to minimize profit distributions (not without risk and also taxable).

Sell the business anyway and watch half the money go to your absentee co-founder (infuriating).

Sound familiar?
There’s a Better Way
If you must bring in a co-owner, treat it like a prenup. Set clear expectations, outline exit terms, and protect the business if things go sideways. (Yes, I draft those kinds of documents all the time.)
But if you’re early in the game—building or buying a business—try literally anything else before giving away equity. Gift cards. Cash. Consulting fees. Free snacks. Future bonuses. Whatever. Just don’t give away the whole farm because you’re short on cash.
You’ll thank me later. Your lawyer will thank you now.
To deals that stay drama-free,
Sara Sharp
Partner, SK&S Law Group
Founder, Deal Academy
